A close reading for the week

“To be, or not to be”

Hamlet · Act 3, Scene 1

The speech is famous because it seems to offer a single question. Its sentences do something less settled: they test an answer, revise it, raise the stakes and stop themselves, and they never once say “I”.

To be, or not to be, that is the question:1
Whether ’tis nobler in the mind2

  1. 1

    No “I”

    The infinitives make the opening feel general: “to be”, where Hamlet might have said “shall I live?” In thirty-three lines the speech never uses “I” or “me”; its pronouns are “we” and “us”, its examples anyone’s. Hamlet thinks about his own life and death in the grammar of a philosophical proposition, which is his brilliance and also his way of keeping the question at arm’s length. Nothing in the speech mentions Claudius, the Ghost or revenge.

  2. 2

    A moral ranking

    “Nobler” asks which choice has greater worth. Hamlet starts with honour, before happiness or relief: he weighs suffering and resistance as rival claims about it, and locates the contest “in the mind”, where nobility cannot be seen or proved. The question of what a noble action would even look like shadows the whole play.
